steps.body: Testing whether a number is a multiple uses the same division: if it divides exactly, counting reaches it; if not, counting steps past.
steps.narration: Testing whether a number is a multiple uses the same division: if it divides exactly, counting reaches it; if not, counting steps past.

widget.prompt: Is 40 a multiple of 8? Count by 8s and check.

commonLandings.feedback: Four hops reach 32; one more is needed to test 40.

widget.missFeedback: Five hops of 8 are needed to reach 40.
widget.successFeedback: 40 — five hops of 8 land exactly on it, so 40 is a multiple of 8.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — five hops of 8 are needed to reach 40.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — counting by 8s hits 40 exactly on the fifth hop.

predict.prompt: 6 is a factor of 24. Is 24 a multiple of 6?
predict.reveal: The two statements say the same thing from opposite ends: 6 × 4 = 24 makes both true at once.

cml.actionGoal: Build the arrangements a number allows, and read the rule that generates the next term for g4pf is multiple.
invariants: A factor pair is a rectangle a number can build and a multiple is a landing a count reaches, so every claim about g4pf is multiple can be settled by construction rather than recall.
misconceptions: Reading an additive gap as a multiplier, stopping a factor search before the pairs repeat, or treating 1 as prime.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Which numbers would make this rectangle impossible to build with whole-number sides?

widget.prompt: Which of these is a multiple of 4?

options.feedback: Correct — counting by 4 lands exactly on 24, so it is 4 taken a whole number of times.
Counting by 4 steps straight past 11; it sits between two multiples rather than on one.
Counting by 4 steps straight past 14; it sits between two multiples rather than on one.
Counting by 4 steps straight past 18; it sits between two multiples rather than on one.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a factor of 40?

options.feedback: Correct — 40 ÷ 20 comes out even, so 20 pairs with another whole number to build 40.
40 ÷ 3 leaves a remainder, so 3 cannot be one side of a whole-number rectangle with area 40.
40 ÷ 6 leaves a remainder, so 6 cannot be one side of a whole-number rectangle with area 40.
40 ÷ 7 leaves a remainder, so 7 cannot be one side of a whole-number rectangle with area 40.

widget.prompt: A rectangle has one side 9 and an area of 81. What is the other side?

commonErrors.feedback: That subtracted the known side. A rectangle's sides MULTIPLY to the area, so divide instead.
81 is the whole area; the question asks for the side that pairs with 9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Test whole-number divisions, or apply the rule once more from the term before.
